Text: The optic canal and the foramina rotundum, ovale, and spinosum all pierce the {{c1::sphenoid::bone}} bone.
Back Extra: Why: the sphenoid sits in the middle of the cranial floor, right where the nerves for the eye and face leave the skull (and where the middle meningeal artery enters through the foramen spinosum).

Text: The foramen magnum and the hypoglossal canals are openings in the {{c1::occipital::bone}} bone.
Back Extra: Why: the occipital bone forms the back of the cranial floor, where the spinal cord (foramen magnum) and the tongue's nerve (hypoglossal canal) leave the skull.

Text: The cribriform foramina perforate the cribriform plate of the {{c1::ethmoid::bone}} bone.
Back Extra: Why: 'cribriform' means sieve-like; dozens of tiny holes let the smell (olfactory) nerve fibers pass up from the nose to the brain.

Text: The internal acoustic meatus is an opening in the {{c1::temporal::bone}} bone.
Back Extra: Why: the inner ear is housed entirely inside the temporal bone, so the nerves for hearing and balance (with the facial nerve) enter the bone through the internal acoustic meatus.

Text: The jugular foramen lies between the {{c1::temporal}} and {{c1::occipital}} bones.
Back Extra: Why: the jugular foramen is the gap left where the two bones meet at the back of the cranial floor; the internal jugular vein and cranial nerves IX, X, and XI leave through it.

Text: The sella turcica is part of the {{c1::sphenoid::bone}} bone.
Back Extra: Why: the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped pocket ('Turkish saddle') in the middle of the cranial floor, holds and protects the pituitary gland.
